title: Week by week
text:
Reading the cadence
Quizzes fall in weeks 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13 and each covers only the material since the previous one; the lowest of six is dropped. Project deliverables land roughly every two to three weeks from week 3 onward, and the heaviest stretch is weeks 9 to 13, when the pilot analysis, final survey and final report overlap with HW8 to HW12 and three quizzes. Week 14 is Thanksgiving with no class but the final survey in the field, so the final analysis cannot start until the data lands; that is the tightest link in the critical path.

The brief for this one was a team project tracker for the semester: activities, a critical path, week-by-week progress, dev logs, and a context bank that knows the course deadlines.

title: Kickoff: the tracker site exists
text: Class 2 was the agentic workflows session: open a folder in Positron, run an agent in it, build a Quarto website, switch the output folder to docs, push, and publish it with GitHub Pages. The brief for this one was a team project tracker for the semester: activities, a critical path, week-by-week progress, dev logs, and a context bank that knows the course deadlines.

title: Kickoff: the tracker site exists
text:
What was built
A Quarto website with output-dir: docs and execute-dir: project. Three CSVs in data/ hold the facts: deadlines.csv (every dated item on the course calendar), weeks.csv (the sixteen class weeks with the project focus and a progress note for each), and activities.csv (forty activities from team formation to the final presentation, each with an owner, start, due, dependencies, a critical-path flag and a status). R code in R/helpers.R reads them and every page is a table or a summary computed from them, so the home page dashboard, the activity list, the float calculation on the critical path and the week table all update from a CSV edit and a re-render. The context bank pages hold the course facts that are safe to publish: grading weights, the deliverable requirements and rubric points, the toolchain and the conventions the professor grades on.

title: Kickoff: the tracker site exists
text:
How it was verified
The site was rendered end to end with Quarto and R before the first commit, and the dates were checked line by line against the course schedule the professor publishes (the tracked date for each project deliverable is the earlier of the two dates the course materials show). The activity count on the home page matches nrow(activities), and the critical-path table lists a successor for every activity that has one.

title: Context bank
text: The context bank is the standing knowledge behind the tracker: what the course is, when everything is due, what each deliverable must contain and how it is scored, who is on the team and who owns which account, and the conventions the professor grades on. It exists so that nobody (person or agent) has to re-derive these facts from the syllabus every time, and so that a fresh Claude Code session in this repo can read CLAUDE.md, then these pages, and be useful within a minute.

title: Context bank
text:
What does not belong here
This site is public because GitHub Pages needs a public repo. So: no grades or feedback, no email addresses, netIDs or phone numbers, no credentials of any kind (Supabase keys and shinyapps tokens live in a .Renviron on one teammate’s machine and nowhere else), and nothing about anyone’s work outside the course. If a fact fails that test it stays in a private place and this site links to nothing.

title: The course
text: EMSE 6035 teaches how to use choice-based conjoint surveys and discrete choice models to inform design decisions for a new product, technology or policy. Class meets Wednesdays in Tompkins 201, in person, attendance taken. Nearly all the work is done in R with an AI agent alongside, and the course is explicit that the agent’s output has to be verified by the student: the final exam opens with an AI-written conjoint analysis that has to be audited. The semester project (45 percent) runs the whole term in teams of 3 to 4 and ends with a reproducible HTML report and a ten-minute presentation.

title: The course
section: The loop the course runs on
text:
The loop the course runs on
Prompt, read the diff, verify, commit and push. The agent almost never makes a syntax mistake, so a wrong answer arrives looking exactly like a right one; running is not the same as right. The three habits the course teaches for working safely: ask for code rather than results, run sanity checks the agent cannot fake (row counts, duplicates, spot checks against the source, NA handling, totals that make sense), and use fake data with the same columns when the real data cannot be shared.

section: R and Quarto habits from the course
text:
R and Quarto habits from the course

Open folders, not files: Positron sets the working directory to the opened folder, so relative paths work. On this site _quarto.yml also sets execute-dir: project, so every page reads data with file.path("data", "file.csv") from the repo root.
Paths with file.path(), relative to the opened folder. Never change the working directory from code, never absolute paths, never here() in student files.
No .Rproj files; the course templates ship them and the instruction is to ignore them.
Every report renders cleanly before it is committed; a .qmd that does not render is not submitted.
Charts: informative titles that state the finding, real axis labels, a source caption, white background, direct labels where possible (the my-chart-style skill from week 2 encodes this).
Ask the agent for code, not answers; keep the data, script, figure pipeline; sanity-check row counts, duplicates, NA handling and totals yourself.

title: Conventions
text:
Git habits
Commit messages say what changed and why (“Add pilot power analysis”, not “update”). Pull before push when someone else may have pushed. Never force-push, never rewrite main. Nothing personal and no credentials in this repo: it is public.

title: Conventions
section: Working with an agent in this repo
text:
Working with an agent in this repo
CLAUDE.md in the repo root is the standing brief for Claude Code (or any agent) opened in this folder. It says what the site is, how to render it, what to edit for each kind of change, and the privacy line. Read it, then this context bank, before making changes; after a session, write a dev log entry and update the activity statuses.

title: Project requirements
text: Teams of 3 to 4 develop quantitative models of consumer choice to inform design decisions for a novel product, technology or policy, in three phases: proposal; pilot survey and analysis; final survey and analysis. The professor wants the result to be portfolio-worthy. Every deliverable is submitted by pushing to the team’s GitHub repo by 11:59 pm on the due date, one submitter per deliverable.

title: Project requirements
text: Teams of 3 to 4 develop quantitative models of consumer choice to inform design decisions for a novel product, technology or policy, in three phases: proposal; pilot survey and analysis; final survey and analysis. The professor wants the result to be portfolio-worthy. Every deliverable is submitted by pushing to the team’s GitHub repo by 11:59 pm on the due date, one submitter per deliverable.

title: Project requirements
section: Selecting a topic (all seven must hold)
text:
Selecting a topic (all seven must hold)







Criterion
Meaning




Innovative or emerging
A new product or technology whose attributes may be competitive but whose market adoption is still uncertain


Well-defined
The course models design decisions; there is no time for conceptual design


Identified target market
A market exists, competitors are known, the competing attributes can be identified, and representative potential customers can be surveyed


Prior to mass commercialization
Only recently or not yet introduced to the mass market


Moderate scope and complexity
Not a commodity like sugar; not a vehicle


Expertise
Reliable access to experts if specialized knowledge is needed


Decision variables
Several non-trivial design decisions the models will inform



The default respondent pool is paid U.S. Prolific participants, so a product U.S. consumers can evaluate is much easier to field. Policy projects are allowed with an alternative structure (problem, policy options, target population, policy attributes).

title: Project requirements
section: Rules common to every written deliverable
text:
Rules common to every written deliverable
Clear, concise, logically structured writing; proof-read with spelling::spell_check_files("file.qmd"); every figure, table and equation referenced in the text; a YAML title and all teammates’ names in author; the template’s explanatory text deleted; an Attribution section (or “All members contributed equally”). Team members who do not contribute meaningfully do not receive the same grade.

1. Proposal (55 points)
Sections, each its own heading: Abstract (what product, what attributes set it apart, what research questions); Introduction (description, background, a picture or diagram); Market Opportunity with Identify Your Customer, Identify Competitors, Identify Market Size; Product Attributes (2 to 4 key attributes, described, quantified, with level ranges, labelled on the diagram and summarised in a table); Research Questions (2 to 3 central design decisions and how they relate to the attributes); Other Questions (at least three outstanding questions and how they will be answered); Attribution. Rubric: Organization and Formatting 5, Abstract 5, Introduction 5, Market Opportunity 10, Product Attributes 10, Research Questions 10, Questions 5, Writing Quality 5. Feedback comes in the week 4 workshop; some teams are asked to narrow scope.


2. Survey Plan (35 points)
Target population (ideal, fallback, exact eligibility question text; default Prolific U.S. general population; other channels if any); attributes and levels for the choice questions (the exact choice question text and a table of attributes, levels, units); survey content (welcome text, consent text restricting to 18 and older and including “I have read and understand the above information”, education material for each attribute, critical respondent information questions, other questions, all as exact text); Attribution. Rubric: Organization and Formatting 5, Target Population 10, Attributes and Levels 10, Survey Content 10.


3. Pilot Survey (35 points)
Built in surveydown from the conjoint buttons template: code/1_make_choice_questions.R generates data/choice_questions.csv with cbc_design; survey.qmd holds welcome, consent, eligibility screening, education, randomised conjoint questions and other questions; app.R runs the Shiny app. Supabase stores the data; the survey is deployed on shinyapps.io from one teammate’s account. Classmates take it in week 9 and leave anonymous feedback. Rubric: Organization and Formatting 5, Survey Content 10, Conjoint Questions 10 (randomised questions render live without error), Deployment 10.


4. Pilot Analysis (35 points)
Download with sd_get_data(), save raw data, clean to long format in clean-data.R, estimate preliminary models in modeling.R, run a power analysis in power-analysis.R. Report sections: Abstract; Introduction; Survey Design (eligibility, respondent information, education, attributes and levels justified, alternatives per question and questions per respondent, no-choice meaning, an example choice question); Pilot Data Analysis with Sample Description, Data Cleaning, Modeling (utility model in LaTeX, coefficient table with standard errors, coefficient figures with uncertainty), Power Analysis; Changes to Final Survey; Attribution; Appendix (full survey). Rubric: Organization and Formatting 5, Pilot Analysis 10, Report Contents 15, Appendix 5.


5. Final Survey (35 points)
The pilot survey with the changes from the pilot analysis, redeployed, all referenced files on the web, plus the eligibility text the professor needs to pre-screen Prolific respondents. Rubric: Organization and Formatting 5, Survey Content 10, Conjoint Questions 10, Deployment 10.


6. Final Analysis Report (40 points, 15 percent of the grade)
A fully reproducible HTML report written as narrative paragraphs. Minimum analysis: clean_data.R to long format; modeling.R with a simple logit on all attributes, a mixed logit with random parameters and at least one sub-group comparison; analysis.R with WTP for every attribute (mean and 95 percent CI, plotted on a common scale), at least one market simulation against competitors with a plot, and sensitivity of market share to price and to other attributes with plots including at least one tornado plot. Sections: Abstract; Introduction; Survey Design; Data Analysis (sample description table, cleaning, modeling with the utility model in LaTeX and a coefficient table); Results; Final Recommendations and Conclusions; Limitations; Attribution; Appendix. Rubric: Organization and Formatting 5, Data Analysis 15, Report Contents 15, Appendix 5.


7. Final Presentation (35 points)
Ten minutes maximum, every member presents at least one slide, slides numbered, title slide with project title, names and date. Content: product introduction, survey overview with an example choice question and a sample-stats slide, main findings with a utility model slide and polished WTP, market simulation and sensitivity charts, a table of simulation attributes, and recommendations. Present live in class on Dec 9 or publish a video and DM the link to the professor on Slack. Rubric: Slide Design 10, Content 15, Communication 10.

title: Critical path
text:
Where the risk concentrates
The two links with no give at all are the pilot-to-final-survey handoff (the pilot analysis is due Nov 1 and the final survey Nov 15, with HW9 and HW10 and Quiz 5 in the same fortnight) and the fielding-to-report link (data arrives during Thanksgiving week and the report is due the Sunday after the final exam). The practical defence is to scaffold clean_data.R, modeling.R and analysis.R on the pilot data in early November so that when the final data lands they only need re-running.
